claims.claim: A longstanding ownership rule exists that software complicates but does not eliminate.
Ownership has historically been limited by safety rules, nuisance laws, and other people's rights.
The established limits on ownership arise from law and coexistence rather than a former owner's continuing command.
A device's sale price reflects the bundle of functions offered with it at the time of sale.
Contract law can support a rule barring sellers from unilaterally removing device functionality after sale.
A party that preserves remote power over a sold device generally designs the relevant system.
A party that preserves remote power over a sold device generally writes the governing terms.
A party that preserves remote power over a sold device generally controls the servers on which the power depends.
Buyers generally lack realistic means to inspect every dependency of a device at checkout.
Clear legal defaults cause ownership to operate as a durable allocation of authority rather than a stack of revocable permissions.
Without effective remedies, disclosure of remote disabling power functions as a smokescreen rather than meaningful buyer protection.
Disclosures of maker-held remote power are generally dense notices that leave buyers with no practical alternative.
Regulators may tend to regard advance notice of remote disabling power as sufficient protection.
Advance notice alone does not rebalance the parties' positions after a device sale is completed.
